analysis.one_liner: Strips federal Clean Water Act protection from small streams, wetlands, and ditches, voiding EPA's water rule.
analysis.headline: The Senate fell three votes short of the 60 needed to begin debate — 57 to 41 — and the bill died without ever coming to a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would throw out the 2015 EPA and Army Corps rule defining which waters the Clean Water Act protects, and require a narrower replacement. The new definition would cover only navigable and interstate waters, mapped drinking-water-source streams, tributaries shown to carry enough pollution to degrade navigable waters, and adjacent protective wetlands. It would exclude streams that flow only after rain, isolated ponds, farm ditches, stormwater and irrigation systems, and prior-converted cropland. It also mandates state and local consultation before any new rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, ranchers, developers, and industrial dischargers who would no longer need federal permits for ditches, farm ponds, seasonal streams, and similar waters, saving permitting time and cost.

how_it_helps.text: Any revision or guidance on the definition of 'waters of the United States' issued after February 4, 2015 would have no force or effect unless it followed the bill's narrower principles, nullifying the agencies' 2015 rule.
The bill excludes from federal jurisdiction groundwater, isolated ponds, ditches and systems for collecting stormwater, wastewater, irrigation, and agricultural water, and prior-converted cropland.
Before any new rule, agencies must consult with governors, state water and agriculture departments, and local governments for at least 180 days, and provide at least a 120-day comment period.
The bill states that it does not limit existing authority to require permits for pollutant discharges into navigable waters or to enforce against unpermitted discharges.

analysis.who_pays: People whose drinking water comes from small upstream streams and wetlands, who would rely on a patchwork of state protections after federal jurisdiction over seasonal streams and many wetlands ends.

drawbacks.text: Discharges into streams that flow only seasonally, and into wetlands not adjacent to covered waters, would no longer require federal permits even where those waters drain toward navigable waters and drinking water supplies.
The new jurisdictional test would depend on flow measures the Army Corps has yet to develop, leaving coverage of many streams uncertain for years.
The committee's Democratic members filed minority views against the bill when it was reported, signaling that its narrowing of the Clean Water Act was contested at the committee stage itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Landowners would gain real relief from federal permitting on ditches, ponds, and seasonal channels, and the mandated state consultation addresses a fair complaint about the 2015 rule's process. The cost is that the headwaters feeding drinking water systems would lose a federal backstop, shifting protection to state rules of varying strength and to a flow test that would take years to build. Weighing honest concerns about overreach against the loss of protection for pollution sources upstream of drinking water, the balance depends heavily on how well each state regulates the waters it would inherit.

outcome.mechanism: A procedural vote to open debate fell three votes short of the 60 needed, Senate Democrats' filibuster held, the motion to proceed was withdrawn, and the bill never reached an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Barrasso with a broad coalition of Republican cosponsors plus Democrats Donnelly, Heitkamp, and Manchin.
The Environment and Public Works Committee reported it favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 16, 2015, with minority views filed, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
On November 3, 2015, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 57-41, short of the 60 votes needed; all 53 voting Republicans backed it, 39 of 44 Democrats opposed it, and both independents voted no.
After the failed vote, the motion to proceed was withdrawn and the bill received no further action before the 114th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People whose drinking water comes from small streams and wetlands kept federal pollution protections; landowners and developers did not get the narrower rule they sought. The underlying 2015 rule remained in effect, though it continued to face court challenges.

sides.party_line_note: On the only recorded vote, all 53 voting Republicans backed moving to the bill while 39 of 44 Democrats and both independents voted no; four Democrats crossed over.

industries.note: The bill excludes farm ditches, farm ponds, manure lagoons, irrigation systems, and prior-converted cropland from federal permitting, cutting compliance costs. Those same waters often drain toward drinking water supplies, so agricultural discharges into them would face no federal check.

Filling or building over seasonal streams and isolated wetlands on project sites would no longer require federal permits, lowering project costs and delays. Downstream communities would absorb the resulting water quality risk.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and industrial dischargers
industries.note: Discharges into ephemeral streams and excluded ponds and ditches would fall outside federal permit and enforcement authority, reducing oversight of pollution that can travel to navigable waters.

The bill keeps mapped drinking-water-source streams under federal protection and promises mapping for certainty, which utilities value. But if upstream seasonal tributaries lose protection, source water quality could suffer.
